review.headline: A Petrov scramble that you won with active rooks in the ending

sections.text: You met the early 4.Bg5 with 4...Be7 and 5...h6, and after 6.Bxf6 Bxf6 the game was balanced. 8...Bh4?! followed by 9...Qxh4 brought your queen out early, but it didn't gain much.
White then went wrong with 12.Bxa6??. After 12...cxd5 the knight on d5 was gone and you stood clearly better (+1.5). The engine wanted 12.Nc3 there.

You gave some of that back with 13...f5?? (+1.3 to -1.0), but 14.exd5? let you hit back with the strong 14...e4!. Then 16...Bxg4?? was another slip; the engine preferred 16...f3. After 17.Qxg4 and the queen trade with 18...Qxe6 19.dxe6, the game went into a rook ending.

The ending is where you shone. Your rooks stayed active (21...Rf5, 29...Rxa3), and 33...Rd5! was the best reply to 33.g4?. After 35...Rxg4 you were clearly better, and 36.f5?? opened the fourth rank so that 36...Rxc4 won a rook.

review.turning_point: 33...Rd5! was the best reply to 33.g4?, and from there your active rooks took over the ending (+3.1 after 35...Rxg4).
review.focus: On 16...Bxg4?? you traded off the bishop and handed the initiative back; the engine's 16...f3 kept the pressure. Before every exchange, ask whether you have a stronger forcing move first.

review.headline: A wild Queen's Pawn game with tactical swings on both sides, ending on the clock while you were better

sections.text: You played 1...d5 2...Nc6 and 4...Nf6 in a calm Catalan-style game. 9...Bb7 was a mistake, because 9...Nxe4 was better, but White replied 10.Nxd6 cxd6!, which was fine and the game stayed balanced.
13...Re7 and 14...a6 drifted a little, and 15.Ng5 was a small mistake by White. Then 17.Nxd6 hit with a discovered attack, but you found 17...Nxf4!, the best reply.
18...Qxb7 was a blunder, as 18...Nxg2 was stronger. The position stayed difficult after 20.c4 Nxb4, which was another blunder, and 21.Bxa8 left you down material.

24.Rc1 was an error by White and 24...Qa2 was a mistake, because 24...Ne2+ was a fork. You fought back with 30...Qxd3!, a skewer that turned the game around, and after 32.Rb1 you were doing well, but you lost on time at move 32.

review.turning_point: 18...Qxb7 and 20...Nxb4 gave back the advantage you earned with 17...Nxf4!.
review.focus: Recapture with care. At 18...Qxb7 the engine wanted 18...Nxg2 first, and your clock ran out in a good position, so use it more evenly.

review.headline: A Damiano Defense where an early weakness left you worse, and a loose queen decided the game

sections.text: You played 2...f6 in the Damiano, which the engine disliked. The position was a bit worse for you after 3.Bc4, and 5...Na5 and 7...Be6 did not fully solve the problems.
8...O-O-O and 9...d5 were mistakes, leaving you with the long castle and an exposed king. You got some chances when White made 10.Qe2 and 11.Na4. 13...Nc6! after 13.Bd2 was a good reply.
15...Qe6 was a bit loose, and 16.Nxc6+ Bxc6 17.b4 set up a threat. 17...Bd6 was the blunder, since 17...Qd7 was needed and you were low on time. After 18.Bxe6 you lost the queen.
The rest was a long defense, with 19.a4, 21.c4 and 23.Nxe5 keeping the pressure on. Your clock ran out at move 24.

review.turning_point: 17...Bd6 left the queen on e6 to be captured by 18.Bxe6.
review.focus: Don't leave your queen on a diagonal where a bishop can take it. At 17...Bd6 the engine wanted 17...Qd7, and watch the clock so you don't make those mistakes in a hurry.

review.headline: A wild bullet clash decided by an unexpected kingside strike

sections.text: Out of the Sicilian Defense, you kept a solid setup until Black erred with 9...Nd4. You punished it immediately by capturing 10.Nxd4 to win a piece, though 14.Nxg7+ handed material back when 14.Bb5+ was much stronger.

The game swung wildly in the complications. On 16...Nc3, Black unleashed a discovered attack on your bishop along with a fork against your queen and rook, but you stabilized with 17.Bxc3 and aimed your pieces at Black's kingside.
Black failed to see your battery after 19.Bd3 and 20.Qe4, allowing 21.Qxh7# for a sudden checkmate.

review.turning_point: Black missed the mate threat after your queen centralized, playing 20...Re5 and letting you deliver 21.Qxh7# instantly.
review.focus: Take an extra moment to check what you leave undefended before moving your queen, as 18.Qd5 left your bishop on e2 open to capture.

review.headline: A sharp Petrov endgame unraveled by loose pieces

sections.text: Out of the opening, 6.Qe2 set up a pin on the e-file and queens quickly traded off into a balanced endgame. However, 12.Bb5?? removed defense from d4 and allowed 12...Bxf3 followed by 13...Nxd4, dropping a pawn. You fought back with active pieces, but 15.Rxd4?? miscalculated the trades, allowing Black to capture your bishop with 15...fxg5.

Black gave you a lifeline when 17...Rxd5?? allowed you to find 18.Rxd5!, pulling the evaluation back near level. Unfortunately, rushing to grab material with 19.Rxg5?? walked straight into the fatal 19...Be3+, losing your rook and ending the game.

review.turning_point: After getting back into the game, 19.Rxg5?? blundered into 19...Be3+, losing a whole rook and forcing resignation.
review.focus: Look for checks and loose pieces before capturing, especially in fast games where 19.Rxg5?? left your rook vulnerable.

review.headline: An unusual opening where White gained space and a hanging rook finished the game

sections.text: After 1.e4 e5 2.d4 you chose 2...Nc6, which is playable but gave White 3.d5 and a space advantage. You rerouted with 3...Nce7 and held the center with 4...d6 and 5...c6.
The pawn moves 8...g5 and 10...a5 were a bit loose, and the engine started to prefer White. 11.Na4 b5 12.Nb6 Ra6 13.Nxc8 Qxc8 simplified, but 14.a3 gave you a chance to equalize.

Then came 15...Rb6, a blunder that put the rook on a square where it could be taken. After 16.Bxb6 you were a rook down. The engine preferred 15...g4, which would have kept things closed on the kingside.

review.turning_point: 15...Rb6 left the rook to be captured by 16.Bxb6.
review.focus: Check whether a square is attacked before moving a rook there. At 15...Rb6 the engine liked 15...g4 instead.

review.headline: A solid Italian game where a good position was decided by the clock after just nine moves

sections.text: You played a sensible Italian Game: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4, followed by 4.O-O, 5.d3 and 6.Nc3. Black answered with 3...d6 and 4...h6, a safe setup, and the position was balanced throughout.
The only inaccuracy was 7.Nd5. It's natural to want to trade, but the engine preferred 7.a4 Be7, which keeps more tension. After 7...Nxd5 8.Bxd5 the evaluation was still close to equal.

You developed well with 9.Be3, and the game was balanced when it ended: you lost on time after only nine moves. This is a clock problem, not a chess one, since your accuracy of 91.6 shows how good your moves were.

review.turning_point: There was no sharp turning point; the game was level when the clock ran out after 9.Be3 Bg4.
review.focus: Watch your clock in the opening. Your moves were good, but at 9.Be3 you had nothing left, so play your first ten moves faster.
